Prevention: Collect and destroy fallen leaves and plant debris by burning.
Pruning of infested twigs and buds.
Spading of surrounding soil of the plant in early
November to expose and kill eggs.
Avoid collection of planting material from infested areas.
Wash tools and clothing after entering areas of known infestations and before entering non- infested areas.
Monitoring: Mealybugs are soft bodied, oval shaped insects covered with waxy white powder.
Males are winged but females are wingless.
Adult females are approximately 15 mm long.
Look for signs/symptoms of giant mealybug feeding:
The insects suck sap from the growing twigs and buds.
They live on twigs and buds in clusters.
They secrete honeydew, on which grows sooty mold fungus which interferes with photosynthesis.
As a result, plants become weak and production can become very low.
Consider direct control actions as soon as mealybugs are identified in your field.
Direct Control: September, destruction of egg sacs through tillage operation of previously affected soil.
Use slippery wrapping tape (7.5 – 10 cm wide) at a height of 1 m so that in
November the newly hatched nymphs cannot climb up, and in late
February, adults from the upper part of the plant cannot climb down to the ground and can easily be collected and destroyed.
Use biopesticides such as potassium salt of fatty acid (Fytoclean @ 8-10 ml/l of water when necessary) directly to the body of the insect.
Restrictions: Avoid spraying broad spectrum synthetic insecticides which might kill beneficial insects or harm the applicator.

When using a pesticide or botanical, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre-harvest interval, max number of sprays, and restricted re-entry interval.
Do not empty into drains and water sources.
